claim: SUMO-modification of nuclear proteins has profound effects on gene expression.
source: SUMO-modification of nuclear proteins has profound effects on gene expression.
evidence: This is a general statement about SUMO modification that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Non-toxic chemical tools that modulate sumoylation in cells are lacking.
source: However, non-toxic chemical tools that modulate sumoylation in cells are lacking.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of the field prior to the study and is supported by the literature review presented in the manuscript.

claim: A cell-based screen was developed that focused on the well-sumoylated substrate, human Liver Receptor Homolog-1 (hLRH-1, NR5A2).
source: Here, to identify small molecule sumoylation inhibitors we developed a cell-based screen that focused on the well-sumoylated substrate, human Liver Receptor Homolog-1 (hLRH-1, NR5A2).
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and implementation of this screening approach.

claim: The primary gene-expression screen assayed two SUMO-sensitive transcripts, APOC3 and MUC1.
source: Our primary gene-expression screen assayed two SUMO-sensitive transcripts, APOC3 and MUC1, that are upregulated by SUMO-less hLRH-1 or by siUBC9 knockdown, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript describes the screening methodology and the specific transcripts used as readouts.

claim: APOC3 and MUC1 are upregulated by SUMO-less hLRH-1 or by siUBC9 knockdown, respectively.
source: Our primary gene-expression screen assayed two SUMO-sensitive transcripts, APOC3 and MUC1, that are upregulated by SUMO-less hLRH-1 or by siUBC9 knockdown, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Tannic acid (TA) emerged as a potent sumoylation inhibitor in vitro with IC50 = 12.8 µM.
source: A polyphenol, tannic acid (TA) emerged as a potent sumoylation inhibitor in vitro (IC50 = 12.8 µM) and in cells.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro sumoylation assay data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: TA is a potent sumoylation inhibitor in cells.
source: A polyphenol, tannic acid (TA) emerged as a potent sumoylation inhibitor in vitro (IC50 = 12.8 µM) and in cells.
evidence: This is supported by cellular assay data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: TA increased hLRH-1 occupancy on SUMO-sensitive transcripts.
source: TA also increased hLRH-1 occupancy on SUMO-sensitive transcripts.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: When tested in humanized mouse primary hepatocytes, TA inhibits hLRH-1 sumoylation.
source: Most significantly, when tested in humanized mouse primary hepatocytes, TA inhibits hLRH-1 sumoylation and induces SUMO-sensitive genes, thereby recapitulating the effects of expressing SUMO-less hLRH-1 in mouse liver.
evidence: This is supported by data from primary hepatocyte experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: TA induces SUMO-sensitive genes in humanized mouse primary hepatocytes.
source: Most significantly, when tested in humanized mouse primary hepatocytes, TA inhibits hLRH-1 sumoylation and induces SUMO-sensitive genes, thereby recapitulating the effects of expressing SUMO-less hLRH-1 in mouse liver.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data from primary hepatocytes shown in Figure 7D.

claim: TA recapitulates the effects of expressing SUMO-less hLRH-1 in mouse liver.
source: Most significantly, when tested in humanized mouse primary hepatocytes, TA inhibits hLRH-1 sumoylation and induces SUMO-sensitive genes, thereby recapitulating the effects of expressing SUMO-less hLRH-1 in mouse liver.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of TA effects with SUMO-less hLRH-1 expression data in Figure 7.

claim: Sumoylation is generally associated with transcriptional repression.
source: SUMO-modification or sumoylation with the Small Ubiquitin-like Modifier (SUMO) is a prevalent post-translational modification of many transcription factors and is generally associated with transcriptional repression (Gill, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gill, 2005.

claim: The sumoylation cycle is multi-stepped and initiated by E1 (SAE1).
source: Similar to other ubiquitin-like modifications, the sumoylation cycle is multi-stepped, as reviewed in Gareau and Lima (2010), and is initiated by E1 (SAE1), which forms a thioester bond with either SUMO-1, 2, or 3.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gareau and Lima (2010).

claim: E1 (SAE1) forms a thioester bond with either SUMO-1, 2, or 3.
source: Similar to other ubiquitin-like modifications, the sumoylation cycle is multi-stepped, as reviewed in Gareau and Lima (2010), and is initiated by E1 (SAE1), which forms a thioester bond with either SUMO-1, 2, or 3.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gareau and Lima (2010).

claim: The single E2 (UBC9) facilitates the hand-off and covalent conjugation of SUMO on a given protein substrate.
source: The single E2 (UBC9) facilitates the hand-off and covalent conjugation of SUMO on a given protein substrate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the sumoylation pathway.

claim: Only E1 and E2 are required for in vitro sumoylation (IVS).
source: Although E3s are believed to guide substrate selectivity in cells, only E1 and E2 are required for in vitro sumoylation (IVS).
evidence: This is established knowledge about in vitro sumoylation assays.

claim: Sumoylation is reversed by sentrin-specific proteases (SENPs).
source: Sumoylation is then reversed by sentrin-specific proteases (SENPs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the sumoylation pathway.

claim: Genetic manipulations that eliminate the sumoylation machinery can result in embryonic lethality or impaired organogenesis.
source: Genetic manipulations that either eliminate the sumoylation machinery or permanently disrupt the normal sumoylation cycle of a substrate can result in embryonic lethality or impaired organogenesis (Flotho and Melchior, 2013; Kang et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2011a; Nacerddine et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sumoylation represents an important, ligand-independent mode to regulate the NR5A nuclear receptor subfamily.
source: Our lab and others find that sumoylation represents an important, ligand-independent mode to regulate the NR5A nuclear receptor subfamily that includes Steroidogenic Factor 1 (NR5A1/SF-1) (Campbell et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2011a; Lee et al., 2005) and Liver Receptor Homolog 1 (NR5A2/LRH-1) (Chalkiadaki and Talianidis, 2005; Stein et al., 2014; Venteclef et al., 2010; Ward et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Knocking-in an unsumoylatable or SUMO-less mutant SF-1 allele leads to profound changes in endocrine physiology and tissue development.
source: For instance, knocking-in an unsumoylatable or SUMO-less mutant SF-1 allele leads to profound changes in endocrine physiology and tissue development (Lee et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2011a.

claim: Even in the presence of one wild-type (WT) allele, the phenotypic effects of SUMO-less SF-1 dominate.
source: Importantly, even in the presence of one wild-type (WT) allele, the phenotypic effects of SUMO-less SF-1 dominate.
evidence: This is based on previous work from the authors' lab.

claim: SUMO-less SF-1 can regulate select downstream targets, which are referred to as SUMO-sensitive.
source: Mechanistically, we find that SUMO-less SF-1 can regulate select downstream targets, which we refer to as SUMO-sensitive (Campbell et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Campbell et al., 2008.

claim: Sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling is ectopically activated after expressing SUMO-less SF-1 in both cells and tissues.
source: Indeed, sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling is ectopically activated after expressing SUMO-less SF-1 in both cells and tissues.
evidence: This is based on previous work from the authors' lab.

claim: The gain-of-function or dominance of the SUMO-less SF-1 mutant leads to expansion of select cell types and hormone imbalance.
source: This gain-of-function or dominance of the SUMO-less SF-1 mutant leads to expansion of select cell types and hormone imbalance, illustrating how disrupting the normal cycle of substrate sumoylation results in disease states.
evidence: This is based on previous work from the authors' lab.

claim: Gain-of-function heterozygous missense mutations in the sumoylation site of microphthalmia-associated transcription factor are tightly linked with some forms of human melanoma.
source: Consistent with our findings, gain-of-function heterozygous missense mutations in the sumoylation site of the transcription factor microphthalmia-associated transcription factor are tightly linked with some forms of human melanoma (Bertolotto et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bertolotto et al., 2011.

claim: SUMO-less variants of the androgen (AR) and glucocorticoid hormone (GR) receptors activate new transcriptional programs linked to cellular proliferation.
source: SUMO-less variants of the androgen (AR) and glucocorticoid hormone (GR) receptors are also reported to activate new transcriptional programs linked to cellular proliferation (Paakinaho et al., 2014; Sutinen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Paakinaho et al., 2014 and Sutinen et al., 2014.

claim: Efforts to drug sumoylation using in vitro target-based assays and in silico screens have identified different classes of SUMO inhibitors with IC50s in the micromolar range.
source: Thus far, efforts to drug sumoylation using in vitro target-based assays and in silico screens have identified different classes of SUMO inhibitors with IC50s in the micromolar range (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by Table 1 which lists various inhibitors and their IC50 values.

claim: Ginkgolic acid (GA) remains the most widely used and commercially available chemical probe targeting general sumoylation.
source: While GA remains the most widely used and commercially available chemical probe targeting general sumoylation, its efficacy as an inhibitor can vary greatly depending on the assay and substrate being tested (Bogachek et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2013; Tossidou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The efficacy of GA as an inhibitor can vary greatly depending on the assay and substrate being tested.
source: While GA remains the most widely used and commercially available chemical probe targeting general sumoylation, its efficacy as an inhibitor can vary greatly depending on the assay and substrate being tested (Bogachek et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2013; Tossidou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bogachek et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2013; Tossidou et al., 2014.

claim: Sumoylation of hLRH-1 occurs primarily in the flexible hinge domain on two major conserved acceptor lysines K192 and K270, with a minor site located in the N-terminal region at K44.
source: Sumoylation of hLRH-1 occurs primarily in the flexible hinge domain on two major conserved acceptor lysines K192 and K270, with a minor site located in the N-terminal region at K44 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1A which shows the schematic of hLRH-1 with sumoylation sites.

claim: hLRH-1 is efficiently sumoylated (~30%) in human placental choriocarcinoma JEG3 and hepatocellular carcinoma HepG2 cells expressing Flag-hLRH-1.
source: Similar to our prior results obtained with SF-1, hLRH-1 is efficiently sumoylated (~30%) in human placental choriocarcinoma JEG3 and hepatocellular carcinoma HepG2 cells expressing Flag-hLRH-1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Multiple sumoylated hLRH-1 species are readily detected with only the endogenous SUMOylation machinery and without the need to add exogenous SUMO or UBC9.
source: Importantly, multiple sumoylated hLRH-1 species are readily detected with only the endogenous SUMOylation machinery and without the need to add exogenous SUMO or UBC9.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Substituting lysines K192 and K270 with arginines (K192R/K270R or 2KR) eliminates nearly all sumoylated LRH-1 species.
source: Substituting lysines K192 and K270 with arginines (K192R/K270R or 2KR) eliminates nearly all sumoylated LRH-1 species, as previously noted (Chalkiadaki and Talianidis, 2005; Lee et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2009) and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In vivo sumoylation of hLRH-1 is robust in mouse liver humanized to express wild-type hLRH-1 (WT).
source: In vivo sumoylation of hLRH-1 is also equally robust, as observed in mouse liver humanized to express wild-type hLRH-1 (WT) (Figure 1B), following viral-mediated infection with recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 8 (AAV8) (Cotugno et al., 2012; Ill et al., 1997) and Figure 1C,D—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and related supplementary figures.

claim: The extent and pattern of hLRH-1 sumoylation in mouse liver are identical to those found in cultured cell lines.
source: Impressively, the extent and pattern of hLRH-1 sumoylation in mouse liver are identical to those found in cultured cell lines, demonstrating for the first time that hLRH-1 is efficiently sumoylated at multiple lysines in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data from Figure 1A and Figure 1B.

claim: hLRH-1 is efficiently sumoylated at multiple lysines in vivo.
source: Impressively, the extent and pattern of hLRH-1 sumoylation in mouse liver are identical to those found in cultured cell lines, demonstrating for the first time that hLRH-1 is efficiently sumoylated at multiple lysines in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expressing SUMO-less hLRH-1 (2KR) eliminates nearly all hLRH-1 sumoylation in mouse liver.
source: By contrast, expressing SUMO-less hLRH-1 (2KR) eliminates nearly all hLRH-1 sumoylation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: APOC3 can be directly regulated by LRH-1.
source: Interestingly, APOC3 can be directly regulated by LRH-1 (Hwang-Verslues and Sladek, 2008), whereas MUC1 is regulated by the androgen receptor (Rajabi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hwang-Verslues and Sladek, 2008.

claim: MUC1 is regulated by the androgen receptor.
source: Interestingly, APOC3 can be directly regulated by LRH-1 (Hwang-Verslues and Sladek, 2008), whereas MUC1 is regulated by the androgen receptor (Rajabi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rajabi et al., 2011.

claim: Expression of CYP11A1 is unaffected by both SUMO-less LRH-1 and siUBC9 knockdown.
source: In contrast, expression of a well-known NR5A downstream target gene, CYP11A1 is unaffected by both SUMO-less LRH-1 and siUBC9 knockdown and is thus designated as a SUMO-insensitive LRH-1 target (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CYP11A1 is designated as a SUMO-insensitive LRH-1 target.
source: In contrast, expression of a well-known NR5A downstream target gene, CYP11A1 is unaffected by both SUMO-less LRH-1 and siUBC9 knockdown and is thus designated as a SUMO-insensitive LRH-1 target (Figure 2B).
evidence: This designation is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The primary screen yielded 13 drugs producing significant changes in MUC1 and APOC3 expression, representing a 0.8% hit rate.
source: A scatter plot of Z-scores ± 2SD from the primary screen shows 13 drugs producing significant changes in MUC1 and APOC3 expression (up and down), representing a 0.8% hit rate (Figure 2C and Source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the scatter plot shown in Figure 2C.

claim: After filtering out drugs resulting in cytotoxicity or changing TBP expression, six potential hits remained.
source: Drugs resulting in cytotoxicity or changing TBP expression were then filtered out leaving six potential hits listed in Table 2.
evidence: This is supported by Table 2 which lists the top six hits.

claim: Only TA emerged as a valid hit from the primary screen, showing significant induction of APOC3 and MUC1, but not CYP11A1.
source: All potential nontoxic candidates were repurchased and tested in a dose response for induction of the two SUMO-sensitive genes used in the primary assay. Only TA emerged as a valid hit from the primary screen, showing significant induction of APOC3 and MUC1, but not CYP11A1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The dose-dependent effects of TA on APOC3 are lost when tested with the SUMO-less hLRH-1 (3KR).
source: On the other hand, the dose-dependent effects of TA on APOC3 are lost when tested with the SUMO-less hLRH-1 (3KR), demonstrating that activation of APOC3 by TA depends on the ability of hLRH-1 to be sumoylatable.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Activation of APOC3 by TA depends on the ability of hLRH-1 to be sumoylatable.
source: On the other hand, the dose-dependent effects of TA on APOC3 are lost when tested with the SUMO-less hLRH-1 (3KR), demonstrating that activation of APOC3 by TA depends on the ability of hLRH-1 to be sumoylatable.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing loss of TA effect with SUMO-less hLRH-1.

claim: APOC3 upregulation by TA depends on hLRH-1.
source: Further, APOC3 upregulation by TA depends on hLRH-1; TA failed to change APOC3 alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effects of TA on MUC1 levels are largely independent of hLRH-1.
source: On the other hand, the effects of TA on MUC1 levels are largely independent of hLRH-1, implying that TA can act more broadly on non-hLRH-1 SUMO-sensitive targets.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TA can act more broadly on non-hLRH-1 SUMO-sensitive targets.
source: On the other hand, the effects of TA on MUC1 levels are largely independent of hLRH-1, implying that TA can act more broadly on non-hLRH-1 SUMO-sensitive targets.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TA affects MUC1 independently of hLRH-1.

claim: TA treatment markedly reduces levels of sumoylated hLRH-1 in JEG3 cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: The transcriptional effects of TA correlated well with the dose-dependent inhibition of hLRH-1 sumoylation in cells, as evidenced by a ~40–50% decrease in all hLRH-1 sumoylated species at 10 µM TA (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At 10 µM TA, there is a ~40–50% decrease in all hLRH-1 sumoylated species.
source: The transcriptional effects of TA correlated well with the dose-dependent inhibition of hLRH-1 sumoylation in cells, as evidenced by a ~40–50% decrease in all hLRH-1 sumoylated species at 10 µM TA (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Diminished hLRH-1 sumoylation is observed only after TA and GA treatment.
source: Diminished hLRH-1 sumoylation is observed only after TA and GA treatment; the other published sumoylation inhibitor, 2',3',4'-trihydroxyflavone (2-D08) (Kim et al., 2013), and another top screening hit, trifluridine (Tri), failed to show similar results (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 2-D08 and trifluridine failed to diminish hLRH-1 sumoylation.
source: Diminished hLRH-1 sumoylation is observed only after TA and GA treatment; the other published sumoylation inhibitor, 2',3',4'-trihydroxyflavone (2-D08) (Kim et al., 2013), and another top screening hit, trifluridine (Tri), failed to show similar results (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: GA appears more effective than TA at reducing hLRH-1 sumoylation in JEG3 cells.
source: However, while GA appears more effective than TA at reducing hLRH-1 sumoylation in JEG3 cells (Figure 3D), this compound leads to significant cytotoxicity beginning at 10 µM after 5 hr (Figure 3E) and 24 hr exposure (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: GA leads to significant cytotoxicity beginning at 10 µM after 5 hr.
source: However, while GA appears more effective than TA at reducing hLRH-1 sumoylation in JEG3 cells (Figure 3D), this compound leads to significant cytotoxicity beginning at 10 µM after 5 hr (Figure 3E) and 24 hr exposure (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: TA is nontoxic even at higher concentrations.
source: By contrast, TA is nontoxic even at higher concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The pattern of sumoylated FL-hLRH-1 in vitro is identical to that found in cells and in vivo.
source: In our assay conditions, the pattern of sumoylated FL-hLRH-1 in vitro is identical as that found in cells and in vivo, and collapses down to a single unmodified band after addition of SENP1 (Figure 4A and refer back to Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data from Figure 4A and Figure 1.

claim: Sumoylated FL-hLRH-1 collapses down to a single unmodified band after addition of SENP1.
source: In our assay conditions, the pattern of sumoylated FL-hLRH-1 in vitro is identical as that found in cells and in vivo, and collapses down to a single unmodified band after addition of SENP1 (Figure 4A and refer back to Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TA is the most effective sumoylation inhibitor when compared to 2-D08 and GA in IVS assays.
source: Using IVS conditions that achieve ~50% sumoylation of FL-hLRH-1, TA is the most effective sumoylation inhibitor when compared to 2-D08 and GA, as well as other candidate hits, (Figure 4B), with an apparent IC50 of 12.8 µM (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by IVS assay data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: TA inhibits and impairs the rate of sumoylation of recombinant hinge-LBD SF-1.
source: As predicted from our initial cellular data, TA inhibits and impairs the rate of sumoylation of other substrates, including recombinant hinge-LBD SF-1, full-length IκBα, and an AR peptide (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: TA inhibits and impairs the rate of sumoylation of full-length IκBα.
source: As predicted from our initial cellular data, TA inhibits and impairs the rate of sumoylation of other substrates, including recombinant hinge-LBD SF-1, full-length IκBα, and an AR peptide (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: TA inhibits and impairs the rate of sumoylation of an AR peptide.
source: As predicted from our initial cellular data, TA inhibits and impairs the rate of sumoylation of other substrates, including recombinant hinge-LBD SF-1, full-length IκBα, and an AR peptide (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: TA impairs E1 thioester formation in non-reducing conditions.
source: As found for davidiin, another tannin sumoylation inhibitor (Takemoto et al., 2014), TA impairs E1 thioester formation in non-reducing conditions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: TA inhibits FL-hLRH-1 sumoylation even in the presence of detergent.
source: Even in the presence of 0.01% Triton X-100, FL-LRH-1 sumoylation was inhibited by TA treatment, as shown in Figure 4E.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The inhibitory effects of TA are not due to non-specific aggregate formation.
source: That TA maintains its inhibitory activity with this detergent suggests that in these assay conditions, the inhibitory effects of TA are not due to non-specific aggregate formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TA remains active in the presence of detergent.

claim: TA is much more efficient at decreasing levels of sumoylated hLRH-1 in HepG2 cells when compared to a nontoxic dose of GA (10 µM) or 2-D08.
source: When compared to a nontoxic dose of GA (10 µM) or 2-D08, TA is much more efficient at decreasing levels of sumoylated hLRH-1 and shows little cytotoxicity in HepG2 cells after longer exposure times (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: TA shows little cytotoxicity in HepG2 cells after longer exposure times.
source: When compared to a nontoxic dose of GA (10 µM) or 2-D08, TA is much more efficient at decreasing levels of sumoylated hLRH-1 and shows little cytotoxicity in HepG2 cells after longer exposure times (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Despite a substantial loss of UBC9 transcripts (95%) and protein (60%) following siRNA-mediated knockdown for 72 hr, hLRH-1 remained fully sumoylated.
source: Surprisingly, despite a substantial loss of UBC9 transcripts (95%) and protein (60%) following siRNA-mediated knockdown for 72 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), hLRH-1 remained fully sumoylated (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Levels of hLRH-1 sumoylation decreased in a dose-dependent manner with TA in HepG2 cells.
source: On the other hand, levels of hLRH-1 sumoylation decreased in a dose-dependent manner with TA (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The higher migrating sumoylated hLRH-1 species in HepG2 cells that diminish with TA were authenticated as SUMO1 or SUMO2 species.
source: The higher migrating sumoylated hLRH-1 species in HepG2 cells that diminish with TA were authenticated as SUMO1 or SUMO2 species (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 1x-Su-hLRH-1 appears to be exclusively modified by SUMO1.
source: Interestingly, 1x-Su-hLRH-1 appears to be exclusively modified by SUMO1, whereas higher Su-hLRH-1 species are modified by SUMO2.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Higher Su-hLRH-1 species are modified by SUMO2.
source: Interestingly, 1x-Su-hLRH-1 appears to be exclusively modified by SUMO1, whereas higher Su-hLRH-1 species are modified by SUMO2.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Both siUBC9 and TA inhibit global sumoylation.
source: Both siUBC9 and TA inhibit global sumoylation, but in this setting, siUBC9 is slightly more effective (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In HepG2 cells, siUBC9 is slightly more effective than TA at inhibiting global sumoylation.
source: Both siUBC9 and TA inhibit global sumoylation, but in this setting, siUBC9 is slightly more effective (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Neither TA nor siUBC9 changes the pool of ubiquitinated proteins.
source: As expected, neither TA nor siUBC9 changes the pool of ubiquitinated proteins.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: TA decreases levels of sumoylated hSF-1 in H295R cells.
source: Instead, we used human adrenal carcinoma H295R cells that express high levels of endogenous hSF-1 and found that similar to exogenously expressed hLRH-1, TA decreases levels of sumoylated hSF-1 in H295S cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: TA is a nontoxic potent global sumoylation inhibitor.
source: Taken together, these data show that TA is a nontoxic potent global sumoylation inhibitor.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective data showing TA's effects on multiple substrates and its low cytotoxicity.

claim: TA regulates CYP24A1, PFKFB3, and SERPINE1 in a dose-dependent manner in HepG2 cells.
source: TA regulates all three genes in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: TA increases hLRH-1 occupancy on LRH-1 binding sites in SERPINE1 proximal promoter region and an intronic site in CYP24A1.
source: Moreover, using ChIP-qPCR we find a significant increase in hLRH-1 occupancy on these LRH-1 binding sites, as shown for a site in the SERPINE1 proximal promoter region and also for an intronic site in CYP24A1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: TA modulates and increases recruitment to SUMO-sensitive hLRH-1 target genes in HepG2 cells.
source: These cellular data suggest that TA modulates and increases recruitment to SUMO-sensitive hLRH-1 target genes in a relevant HepG2 cellular model system.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-qPCR and gene expression data.

claim: Both WT and SUMO-less hLRH-1 upregulate the classic LRH-1 target Cyp8b1.
source: Although WT and SUMO-less hLRH-1 upregulate the classic LRH-1 target Cyp8b1 (Lee et al., 2008), expression of SUMO-less hLRH-1 leads to robust activation of adiponectin (Adipoq) and sonic hedgehog (Shh), in mouse liver (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Expression of SUMO-less hLRH-1 leads to robust activation of adiponectin (Adipoq) and sonic hedgehog (Shh) in mouse liver.
source: Although WT and SUMO-less hLRH-1 upregulate the classic LRH-1 target Cyp8b1 (Lee et al., 2008), expression of SUMO-less hLRH-1 leads to robust activation of adiponectin (Adipoq) and sonic hedgehog (Shh), in mouse liver (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The pattern of hLRH-1 sumoylation is preserved in cultured hepatocytes.
source: The pattern of hLRH-1 sumoylation is preserved in cultured hepatocytes, but lost in primary cultures expressing the SUMO-less hLRH-1 mutant (Figure 7C, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: TA (10 µM, 5 hr) diminishes levels of sumoylated WT hLRH-1 in primary mouse hepatocytes, with nearly all sumoylated species absent including 1x-SUMO-hLRH-1.
source: Importantly, when tested in primary mouse hepatocytes TA (10 µM, 5 hr) diminishes levels of sumoylated WT hLRH-1, with nearly all sumoylated species absent including 1x-SUMO-hLRH-1 (Figure 7C, right panel); thus closely resembling the SUMO-less 2KR mutant.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: TA treatment in primary mouse hepatocytes closely resembles the SUMO-less 2KR mutant.
source: Importantly, when tested in primary mouse hepatocytes TA (10 µM, 5 hr) diminishes levels of sumoylated WT hLRH-1, with nearly all sumoylated species absent including 1x-SUMO-hLRH-1 (Figure 7C, right panel); thus closely resembling the SUMO-less 2KR mutant.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of TA-treated and 2KR mutant data.

claim: TA switches on Shh, Gli2, and Adipoq in mouse primary hepatocytes that express only endogenous mLRH-1.
source: SUMO-sensitive genes identified in whole liver were then tested with TA in mouse primary hepatocytes that express only endogenous mLRH-1. As found in the liver, Shh, its downstream effector Gli2, and Adipoq are essentially switched on by TA (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The trigger-like effect of TA and SUMO-less hLRH-1 on Shh and Gli2 is consistent with previous findings that hedgehog signaling can be ectopically activated in mouse organs after knocking-in SUMO-less SF-1.
source: This trigger-like effect of TA and SUMO-less hLRH-1 on Shh and Gli2 is consistent with our previous findings that hedgehog signaling can be ectopically activated in mouse organs after knocking-in SUMO-less SF-1 (Lee et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2011a.

claim: Cell viability was unchanged by TA after 24 hr exposure in primary hepatocytes.
source: Importantly, cell viability was unchanged by TA after 24 hr exposure (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In primary cells, TA abrogates hLRH-1 sumoylation and induces hLRH-1 SUMO-sensitive downstream target genes.
source: These data establish that in primary cells, TA abrogates hLRH-1 sumoylation and induces hLRH-1 SUMO-sensitive downstream target genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective data from primary hepatocyte experiments.

claim: TA is a potent inhibitor of hLRH-1 sumoylation in multiple platforms.
source: Here, using a phenotypic, gene-expression-based screen we identify the polyphenol, TA as a potent inhibitor of hLRH-1 sumoylation in multiple platforms.
evidence: This is supported by data from in vitro, cellular, and primary hepatocyte experiments.

claim: In vitro assays confirm that TA impairs substrate sumoylation.
source: In vitro assays confirm that TA impairs substrate sumoylation.
evidence: This is supported by IVS assay data shown in Figure 4.

claim: An acute, nontoxic dose of TA treatment markedly reduces levels of sumoylated hLRH-1 in several cellular model systems.
source: When tested n several cellular model systems, an acute, nontoxic dose of TA treatment markedly reduces levels of sumoylated hLRH-1, as well as hSF-1, and modulates expression of hLRH-1 target genes.
evidence: This is supported by data from JEG3, HepG2, and H295R cells.

claim: TA markedly reduces levels of sumoylated hSF-1 in cellular model systems.
source: When tested n several cellular model systems, an acute, nontoxic dose of TA treatment markedly reduces levels of sumoylated hLRH-1, as well as hSF-1, and modulates expression of hLRH-1 target genes.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: TA modulates expression of hLRH-1 target genes in cellular model systems.
source: When tested n several cellular model systems, an acute, nontoxic dose of TA treatment markedly reduces levels of sumoylated hLRH-1, as well as hSF-1, and modulates expression of hLRH-1 target genes.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 3, 6, and 7.

claim: In primary cultures of mouse hepatocytes, TA inhibits hLRH-1 sumoylation and is able to mimic the transcriptional output of the SUMO-less LRH-1 mutant by switching on genes that have been associated with hepatic injury.
source: Impressively, in primary cultures of mouse hepatocytes, TA inhibits hLRH-1 sumoylation and is able to mimic the transcriptional output of the SUMO-less LRH-1 mutant by switching on genes that have been associated with hepatic injury.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The gene-expression-based screen was designed to sample the transcriptional output of substrate sumoylation.
source: Our gene-expression-based screen was designed to sample the transcriptional output of substrate sumoylation, which has not been possible with in vitro target-based screens.
evidence: This describes the rationale and design of the screening approach.

claim: Assessing transcriptional endpoints makes it possible to integrate other mechanisms that promote substrate-specific sumoylation or desumoylation.
source: We reasoned that assessing transcriptional endpoints makes it possible to integrate other mechanisms that promote substrate-specific sumoylation or desumoylation, including possible synergistic effects of multiple transcription factor sumoylation (Holmstrom et al., 2008; Komatsu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is the authors' reasoning supported by citations.

claim: hLRH-1 is well-sumoylated with a stereotypic pattern of multiple sumoylated species requiring only the endogenous sumoylation machinery when expressed in HEK293S, JEG3, and HepG2 cells, in primary hepatocytes and in liver tissue.
source: Second, hLRH-1 is well-sumoylated with a stereotypic pattern of multiple sumoylated species requiring only the endogenous sumoylation machinery when it is expressed in HEK293S, JEG3, and HepG2 cells, in primary hepatocytes and in liver tissue.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1, 5, and 7.

claim: The findings differ from the need for exogenous SUMO1/2 and E3s required to detect 1x-sumoylated V5-tagged mLRH-1 in HEK293 cells or primary hepatocytes.
source: These findings differ from the need for exogenous SUMO1/2 and E3s required to detect 1x-sumoylated V5-tagged mLRH-1 in HEK293 cells or primary hepatocytes (Stein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from Stein et al., 2014.

claim: When compared to hFXR, the number and intensity of hLRH-1 sumoylated species far exceed the faint, single FXR sumoylated band detected when hFXR is expressed in mouse liver.
source: In addition, when compared to hFXR, another sumoylated hepatic NR, the number and intensity of hLRH-1 sumoylated species far exceed the faint, single FXR sumoylated band detected when hFXR is expressed in mouse liver (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from Kim et al., 2015.

claim: The pattern of hLRH-1 sumoylation is readily duplicated in vitro.
source: Finally, the pattern of hLRH-1 sumoylation is readily duplicated in vitro, allowing one to also test candidate sumoylation modulators in a defined cocktail.
evidence: This is supported by IVS assay data shown in Figure 4.

claim: NR5As might be particularly good substrates for sumoylation because their major acceptor lysines reside in the flexible hinge domain.
source: We posit that NR5As might be particularly good substrates for sumoylation because their major acceptor lysines reside in the flexible hinge domain, possibly promoting strong protein–protein interactions previously observed between Ubc9 and both SF-1 and LRH-1 (Lee et al., 2005).
evidence: This is speculation based on structural features and previous observations.

claim: The residual UBC9 protein following siUBC9 knockdown likely accounts for the persistent levels of 1x SU-LRH-1.
source: Indeed, the residual UBC9 protein following siUBC9 knockdown likely accounts for the persistent levels of 1x SU-LRH-1 and suggests that once UBC9 is charged with SUMO1/2, sumoylation of hLRH-1 proceeds efficiently.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that hLRH-1 remains sumoylated despite UBC9 knockdown.

claim: Once UBC9 is charged with SUMO1/2, sumoylation of hLRH-1 proceeds efficiently.
source: Indeed, the residual UBC9 protein following siUBC9 knockdown likely accounts for the persistent levels of 1x SU-LRH-1 and suggests that once UBC9 is charged with SUMO1/2, sumoylation of hLRH-1 proceeds efficiently.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Inhibiting E2 by 2-D08 is ineffective at blocking hLRH-1 sumoylation.
source: Interestingly, as with siUBC9, inhibiting E2 by 2-D08 is also ineffective at blocking hLRH-1 sumoylation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The consistent and robust sumoylation observed for hLRH-1 were instrumental in facilitating follow-up studies on candidate small molecule hits from the primary screen.
source: Regardless of the underlying mechanisms that confer relatively high basal levels of NR5A sumoylation in cells and in tissues, the consistent and robust sumoylation observed for hLRH-1 were instrumental in facilitating follow-up studies on candidate small molecule hits from our primary screen.
evidence: This is a reflection on the utility of hLRH-1 as a substrate for the screening approach.

claim: The effects of TA in sumoylation assays are extremely reproducible in multiple cell lines and in primary hepatocytes.
source: While polyphenols such as TA are easily dismissed as promiscuous inhibitors and false positives in high-throughput screens (Feng and Shoichet, 2006; Pohjala and Tammela, 2012), the effects of TA in our sumoylation assays are extremely reproducible in multiple cell lines and in primary hepatocytes.
evidence: This is supported by data from multiple experimental platforms.

claim: Other colloid-forming phenolic compounds, such as bergapten and coumarin 153, failed to emerge as hits in the primary screen.
source: Interestingly, although other colloid-forming pehnolic compounds, such as bergapten and coumarin 153 (Pohjala and Tammela, 2012), are present in the Pharmakon library, both failed to emerge as hits in the primary screen.
evidence: This is based on the screening results.

claim: In IVS assay conditions, TA is more effective than either 2-D08 or GA.
source: Indeed, in our IVS assay conditions, TA is more effective than either 2-D08 or GA and can inhibit sumoylation of multiple substrates in vitro, including the hinge-LBD of SF-1, an androgen receptor peptide, and full-length IκBα.
evidence: This is supported by IVS assay data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: TA can inhibit sumoylation of multiple substrates in vitro, including the hinge-LBD of SF-1, an androgen receptor peptide, and full-length IκBα.
source: Indeed, in our IVS assay conditions, TA is more effective than either 2-D08 or GA and can inhibit sumoylation of multiple substrates in vitro, including the hinge-LBD of SF-1, an androgen receptor peptide, and full-length IκBα.
evidence: This is supported by IVS assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The fact that 2-D08 fails to inhibit hLRH-1 sumoylation but is effective on other substrates might reflect that 2-D08 fails to block the strong interactions between Ubc9 and NR5As.
source: The fact that 2-D08 fails to inhibit hLRH-1 sumoylation but is effective on other substrates (AR peptide and FL-IκBα) might reflect the fact that 2-D08 fails to block the strong interactions between Ubc9 and NR5As, as mentioned above.
evidence: This is speculation based on the differential effects of 2-D08 on different substrates.

claim: Mechanistically distinct sumoylation inhibitors act on different classes of substrates.
source: These data imply that mechanistically distinct sumoylation inhibitors act on different classes of substrates.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of various inhibitors on different substrates.

claim: Unlike GA, TA appears to be well-tolerated in both immortalized and primary cell cultures.
source: We also find that unlike GA, which decreases cell viability as shown here and reported by (Liu and Zeng, 2009), TA appears to be well-tolerated in both immortalized and primary cell cultures.
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figures 3E, 5B, and 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: GA might decrease sumoylation as an adaptive response to cell death.
source: Hence, while GA might decrease sumoylation as an adaptive response to cell death, the utility of GA in assessing the transcriptional responses of substrate sumoylation is potentially quite limiting.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of GA's effects.

claim: TA blocks substrate sumoylation by inhibiting E1 thioesterization.
source: Our data suggest strongly that TA blocks substrate sumoylation by inhibiting E1 thioesterization, as found for the ellagitannin, Davidiin (Takemoto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and comparison with Davidiin.

claim: The known aggregate formation and antioxidant properties of TA appear to be less important in inhibiting substrate sumoylation.
source: The known aggregate formation and antioxidant properties of TA appear to be less important in inhibiting substrate sumoylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TA remains active in the presence of detergent.

claim: Two other antioxidants, ellagic acid and EGCG, are ineffective at inhibiting hLRH-1 sumoylation.
source: In this regard, we find that two other antioxidants, ellagic acid and EGCG, are ineffective at inhibiting hLRH-1 sumoylation (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on unpublished data mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Conditions in IVS assays are highly reducing making it unlikely that TA inhibits LRH-1 sumoylation via its antioxidant properties in this setting.
source: Furthermore, conditions in our IVS assays are highly reducing making it unlikely that TA inhibits LRH-1 sumoylation via its antioxidant properties in this setting.
evidence: This is inferred from the assay conditions.

claim: TA is effective at blocking hLRH-1 sumoylation in humanized primary hepatocytes.
source: That TA is effective at blocking hLRH-1 sumoylation in humanized primary hepatocytes greatly strengthens the validity of TA as a useful chemical tool to assess the cellular effects of sumoylation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: TA is more effective at blocking hLRH-1 sumoylation in primary hepatocytes as compared to HepG2 cells where 1x SUMO-hLRH-1 persists even at the highest dose of TA.
source: Interestingly, TA is more effective at blocking hLRH-1 sumoylation in primary hepatocytes as compared to HepG2 cells where 1x SUMO-hLRH-1 persists even at the highest dose of TA; a similar trend was noted for endogenous hSF-1 in H295R cells.
evidence: This is based on comparison of data from Figure 5C and Figure 7C.

claim: The lower efficacy of TA in immortalized cell lines may reflect an increase in the general sumoylation machinery in immortalized versus primary cells.
source: The lower efficacy of TA in immortalized cell lines may reflect an increase in the general sumoylation machinery in immortalized versus primary cells, as noted by (Bellail et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to Bellail et al., 2014.

claim: The ectopic activation of SHH signaling observed in primary hepatocytes after overexpressing SUMO-less hLRH-1 and after TA treatment confirms earlier work showing that elimination of SF-1 sumoylation activates hedgehog signaling in endocrine tissues.
source: The ectopic activation of SHH signaling observed here in primary hepatocytes after overexpressing SUMO-less hLRH-1 and after TA treatment confirms our earlier work showing that elimination of SF-1 sumoylation activates hedgehog signaling in endocrine tissues (Lee et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7 and a citation to Lee et al., 2011a.

claim: Hyperactivation of hedgehog signaling in liver is associated with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) progression and responses to liver injury.
source: Others have noted that hyperactivation of hedgehog signaling in liver is associated with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) progression and responses to liver injury (Grzelak et al., 2014; Guy et al., 2012; Hirsova and Gores, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grzelak et al., 2014; Guy et al., 2012; Hirsova and Gores, 2015.

claim: Adiponectin is an adipocyte-derived protein that reduces fatty liver.
source: Adiponectin is an adipocyte-derived protein that reduces fatty liver (Xu et al., 2003) and appears protective against NASH (Asano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2003 and Asano et al., 2009.

claim: Adiponectin appears protective against NASH.
source: Adiponectin is an adipocyte-derived protein that reduces fatty liver (Xu et al., 2003) and appears protective against NASH (Asano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Asano et al., 2009.

claim: While adiponectin is normally never expressed in liver, hepatic adiponectin transcripts are observed in rats after chemically induced hepatotoxicity.
source: Indeed, while adiponectin is normally never expressed in liver, hepatic adiponectin transcripts are observed in rats after chemically induced hepatotoxicity (Yoda-Murakami et al., 2001) and in patients with fatty liver or fully progressed NASH (Uribe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yoda-Murakami et al., 2001 and Uribe et al., 2008.

claim: Hepatic adiponectin transcripts are observed in patients with fatty liver or fully progressed NASH.
source: Indeed, while adiponectin is normally never expressed in liver, hepatic adiponectin transcripts are observed in rats after chemically induced hepatotoxicity (Yoda-Murakami et al., 2001) and in patients with fatty liver or fully progressed NASH (Uribe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Uribe et al., 2008.

claim: Tipping the balance of the hLRH-1 sumoylation cycle toward desumoylation might initiate adaptive responses to liver injury, and eventually a pro-inflammatory response.
source: The finding that SUMO-less hLRH-1 and TA switch on hepatic adiponectin and hedgehog signaling leads us to speculate that tipping the balance of the hLRH-1 sumoylation cycle toward desumoylation might initiate adaptive responses to liver injury, and eventually a pro-inflammatory response, as suggested by others (Venteclef et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and supported by a citation to Venteclef et al., 2010.

claim: A global knock-in of a single SUMO mutation (K289R) in mouse LRH-1 has no strong phenotype on its own.
source: Interestingly, a global knock-in of a single SUMO mutation (K289R) in mouse LRH-1, which is equivalent to K270R in hLRH-1, has no strong phenotype on its own, but mitigates aortic plaque formation in Ldlr-/- arteriosclerosis-prone mice (Stein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stein et al., 2014.

claim: A global knock-in of K289R in mouse LRH-1 mitigates aortic plaque formation in Ldlr-/- arteriosclerosis-prone mice.
source: Interestingly, a global knock-in of a single SUMO mutation (K289R) in mouse LRH-1, which is equivalent to K270R in hLRH-1, has no strong phenotype on its own, but mitigates aortic plaque formation in Ldlr-/- arteriosclerosis-prone mice (Stein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stein et al., 2014.

claim: Revealing the full physiological consequences of LRH-1 sumoylation could require the elimination of both major sumoylation sites in the flexible hinge domain and the use of conditional knock-in strategies that are specific for the adult liver.
source: Hence, revealing the full physiological consequences of LRH-1 sumoylation could require the elimination of both major sumoylation sites in the flexible hinge domain and the use of conditional knock-in strategies that are specific for the adult liver.
evidence: This is speculation about future experimental approaches.

claim: TA is a useful, nontoxic chemical tool for assessing the transcriptional and cellular effects of sumoylation in both immortalized and primary cell cultures.
source: In summary, using a novel cell-based assay, we report that the commercially derived, plant extract TA is a useful, nontoxic chemical tool for assessing the transcriptional and cellular effects of sumoylation in both immortalized and primary cell cultures.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by all the experimental data.

claim: The ratio of sumoylated to desumoylated substrate can be chemically manipulated to switch on and off sumo-sensitive transcriptional programs.
source: Based on our collective studies that have focused on the sumoylation of NR5As, we propose that the ratio of sumoylated to desumoylated substrate can be chemically manipulated to switch on and off sumo-sensitive transcriptional programs.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the collective findings of the study.
